questions.q: Find the eigenvectors of H = [[3,1],[1,3]].
w: (1,0) with λ = 3 and (0,1) with λ = 3
(1,2)/√5 with λ = 4 and (2,−1)/√5 with λ = 2, rotated
questions.x: Equal diagonal entries put the eigenvectors at 45°: H(1,1) = 4(1,1) and H(1,−1) = 2(1,−1).

questions.q: Match each two-variable quadratic f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx to its contour family
pairs: H singular PSD, b in range of H
H singular PSD, b with null-space part
questions.x: Eigenvalue signs set the family: two positive give ellipses, mixed signs give hyperbolas, and a zero eigenvalue gives a trough that is flat or sloping depending on b along the null direction.

questions.q: x* is a critical point and Hv = λv with ‖v‖ = 1. Substituting x = x* + αv into f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx + c gives
questions.a: f = f(x*) + ½λα²
w: f = f(x*) + λα²
f = f(x*) + ½α²/λ
f = f(x*) + λα + ½λα²
questions.x: ∇f(x*) = 0 removes the linear term and vᵀHv = λ for a unit eigenvector, so f = f(x*) + ½λα² along each eigendirection.

questions.q: f(x,y) = x² + 4xy + y², so H = [[2,4],[4,2]]. Classify the origin.
questions.a: Saddle; f decreases along (1,−1)
w: Minimum; H has positive diagonal
Saddle; f decreases along (1,1)
Maximum; det H is negative
questions.x: The eigenvalues are 6 along (1,1) and −2 along (1,−1), so the origin is a saddle and f falls as −α² along (1,−1).

questions.q: f = ½xᵀHx with H = [[5,3],[3,5]]. Find the length of the longest semi-axis of the contour f = 4.
questions.x: The eigenvalues are 2 and 8; along a unit eigenvector ½λr² = 4 gives r = √(8/λ), so the smallest eigenvalue λ = 2 gives the longest semi-axis r = 2.

questions.q: f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx with H = [[4,2],[2,4]] and b = (−6, −6). Find the minimum value f*.
questions.x: Solving Hx = −b gives x* = (1, 1), and f* = ½bᵀx* = −½bᵀH⁻¹b = −6.

questions.q: Complete the minimum value of a positive definite quadratic f = ½xᵀHx + bᵀx + c
questions.a: H⁻¹
w: H
2H⁻¹
H⁻²
questions.x: Substituting x* = −H⁻¹b gives f* = c − ½bᵀH⁻¹b.

questions.q: For symmetric H, the directional curvature dᵀHd/dᵀd over all nonzero d spans
questions.a: [λ_min, λ_max]
w: [0, λ_max]
[λ_min, trace H]
[−λ_max, λ_max]
questions.x: The Rayleigh quotient is bounded by the extreme eigenvalues and reaches each at its eigenvector.

questions.q: On a plot of φ(α) = f(x + αp), the Armijo condition accepts α where φ(α) lies
questions.a: On or below the line φ(0) + c₁αφ′(0)
w: On or above the line φ(0) + c₁αφ′(0)
Below the tangent line φ(0) + αφ′(0)
On or below the horizontal line φ(0)
questions.x: The Armijo line has a gentler slope c₁φ′(0) than the tangent, and accepted steps lie on or under it.

questions.q: Graphically, the weak curvature condition φ′(α) ≥ c₂φ′(0) accepts steps where
questions.a: The slope has flattened to at least c₂φ′(0)
w: The slope is steeper than it was at α = 0 (more negative)
φ(α) lies below φ(0)
The slope is exactly zero
questions.x: Since φ′(0) < 0 and 0 < c₂ < 1, the condition keeps steps where φ has flattened enough, which excludes tiny steps.

questions.q: Goldstein conditions φ(0) + (1−c)αφ′(0) ≤ φ(α) ≤ φ(0) + cαφ′(0), 0 < c < ½. A known drawback is that
questions.a: Their lower bound can exclude every minimizer of φ
w: They require a gradient evaluation at every single trial step
They require c above ½ for Newton steps
They demand an exact line search each time
questions.x: Goldstein uses only function values, and its lower bound can cut off the minimizers of φ, so Wolfe conditions are preferred for quasi-Newton methods.

questions.q: Backtracking on f(x) = x⁴ from x = 1 along p = −f′(1) = −4, with c₁ = 10⁻⁴, starting at α = 1 and halving. Which α is accepted?
questions.x: α = 1 gives f(−3) = 81 and α = 0.5 gives f(−1) = 1, both above the Armijo line; α = 0.25 gives f(0) = 0, which passes.

questions.q: Steepest descent with exact line search on a quadratic with κ = 99. Using the worst-case factor ((κ−1)/(κ+1))² per iteration, how many iterations reduce f − f* by 10⁶? Round up to an integer.
questions.x: The factor is 0.98² = 0.9604, and ln(10⁻⁶)/ln(0.9604) = 341.9, so 342 iterations.

questions.q: Complete the strong Wolfe curvature condition
questions.a: c₂
w: c₁
1 − c₂
c₂²
questions.x: Strong Wolfe bounds the magnitude of the new directional derivative by c₂ times the initial one, with 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1.

questions.q: Why do the Wolfe conditions require 0 < c₁ < c₂ < 1?
questions.a: So acceptable steps exist for any smooth f bounded below
w: So the first trial step α = 1 always passes
So the curvature condition implies sufficient decrease too
So the line search converges quadratically
questions.x: With c₁ < c₂, an interval of steps satisfying both conditions exists for every smooth f bounded below along a descent direction.

questions.q: Why does a quasi-Newton line search always try α = 1 first?
questions.a: The unit step is eventually accepted, keeping superlinear rate
w: The unit step exactly minimizes φ(α) along every direction p
It satisfies the curvature condition for every smooth function
It guarantees monotone decrease without any further checks at all
questions.x: Near the solution the quasi-Newton step is well scaled, so accepting α = 1 preserves the superlinear convergence rate.

questions.q: Compared with BFGS, the SR1 update
questions.a: May become indefinite, which suits trust region methods
w: Stays positive definite whenever the curvature yᵀs > 0
Is a rank-two update built from both s and Bs vectors
Needs an exact line search to keep its denominator safe
questions.x: SR1 is a symmetric rank-one secant update that can capture negative curvature, which a trust region handles naturally; it is skipped when its denominator is tiny.

questions.q: The DFP update is related to the BFGS update by
questions.a: Swapping s with y and B with its inverse H
w: Using a rank-one correction in place of rank-two
Applying the update only once every n iterations
Adding a ridge term λI to every Hessian update
questions.x: DFP and BFGS are dual: the BFGS formula for B, with s and y interchanged, gives the DFP formula for H = B⁻¹.

questions.q: Complete the BFGS inverse Hessian update, with ρ = 1/(yᵀs)
questions.a: ρssᵀ
w: ρyyᵀ
ρsyᵀ
ssᵀ/(sᵀHs)
questions.x: The ρssᵀ term enforces the inverse secant condition H₊y = s, and the update keeps H₊ positive definite when yᵀs > 0.

questions.q: Linear CG on Ax = b with A = [[4,1],[1,3]], b = (1, 2), x₀ = (2, 1). Compute the first step length α₀ = r₀ᵀr₀ / p₀ᵀAp₀ to 4 decimals.
Pure Newton on f(x) = x⁴ from x₀ = 1. Give x₁ to 4 decimals.
questions.x: x₁ = x₀ − 4x₀³/(12x₀²) = 2x₀/3 = 0.6667; f″(0) = 0 at the minimizer, so Newton converges only linearly here with ratio 2/3.

questions.q: For linear CG on an SPD system, the error in the A-norm shrinks per iteration by roughly
questions.x: The bound ‖e_k‖_A ≤ 2((√κ − 1)/(√κ + 1))ᵏ‖e₀‖_A shows CG depends on √κ, which is why preconditioning pays off.

questions.q: Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) stores
questions.a: The m most recent (s, y) pairs
w: A dense n×n inverse Hessian
Only the diagonal of the Hessian
The last m full Hessian matrices
questions.x: L-BFGS applies the inverse Hessian implicitly through a two-loop recursion over m stored pairs, costing O(mn) memory and work.

questions.q: Match each method to its local convergence behaviour on a smooth strictly convex problem
pairs: Linear CG on an n-dim SPD quadratic
questions.x: Curvature information raises the rate: gradients alone give linear, secant updates give superlinear, the exact Hessian gives quadratic, and CG terminates in n steps on a quadratic.

questions.q: Dogleg with g = (2, 2), B = diag(1, 2), Δ = 2. Compute the step and give its first component p₁.
questions.x: p_U = −(8/12)g = (−4/3, −4/3) with norm 1.886 and p_B = (−2, −1) with norm 2.236; the segment meets ‖p‖ = 2 at τ = 0.4 past p_U, giving p = (−1.6, −1.2).

questions.q: f(x_k) = 10, f(x_k + p) = 7, m(0) = 10 and m(p) = 6. Compute the trust region ratio ρ.
questions.x: ρ = actual reduction / predicted reduction = (10 − 7)/(10 − 6) = 0.75, a good agreement between model and function.

questions.q: Steihaug-CG solves the trust region subproblem with CG on Bp = −g and stops when
questions.a: An iterate leaves the region or negative curvature appears
w: The residual norm first increases between two iterations
The step becomes parallel to the steepest descent direction
The model value rises above m(0) on two consecutive iterations
questions.x: On negative curvature or a boundary crossing, Steihaug-CG moves to the boundary along the current direction; otherwise it stops at a small residual.

questions.q: Standard radius update thresholds (Nocedal and Wright) are
questions.a: Shrink if ρ < ¼; expand if ρ > ¾ and ‖p‖ = Δ
w: Shrink if ρ < ¾; expand if ρ > ¼ and ‖p‖ < Δ
Shrink if ρ < 0; expand whenever ρ > 0
Shrink if ρ > 1; expand if ρ < ½
questions.x: Poor agreement (ρ < ¼) shrinks Δ by a factor of 4, and very good agreement with a boundary step (ρ > ¾) doubles Δ up to Δ_max.

questions.q: Complete the Cauchy point formula, assuming gᵀBg > 0
questions.a: ‖g‖³/(Δ·gᵀBg)
w: ‖g‖²/(gᵀBg)
Δ·gᵀBg/‖g‖³
‖g‖³/(Δ²·gᵀBg)
questions.x: Minimizing the model along −g gives step length ‖g‖²/gᵀBg, and τ caps it at the boundary, so τ = min(1, ‖g‖³/(Δ·gᵀBg)).

questions.q: The exact trust region solution p* satisfies (B + λI)p* = −g together with
questions.a: λ ≥ 0, λ(Δ − ‖p*‖) = 0, B + λI PSD
w: λ ≤ 0, λ(Δ − ‖p*‖) = 0, B − λI PSD
λ ≥ 0, λ = ‖g‖/Δ, B PSD
λ = 0 and ‖p*‖ = Δ always
questions.x: These Moré-Sorensen conditions characterize the global solution of the subproblem, with λ acting as the multiplier on ‖p‖ ≤ Δ.

questions.q: Why can a trust region method work directly with an indefinite B?
questions.a: The bound ‖p‖ ≤ Δ keeps the subproblem well posed
w: An indefinite B always makes the ratio ρ equal to exactly one
The Cauchy point removes negative eigenvalues
Δ is set to the most negative eigenvalue
questions.x: The ball constraint gives a bounded subproblem for any symmetric B, so negative curvature directions are exploited up to the radius.

questions.q: Put one trust region iteration in order
steps: Build the model m(p) from g and B at x_k
Solve the subproblem approximately for p with ‖p‖ ≤ Δ
Evaluate f(x_k + p) and form ρ
Update Δ and accept the step when ρ > η
questions.x: Each iteration builds and solves the model, then compares actual and predicted reduction to set the radius and accept or reject.

questions.q: min x² + y² subject to h = x + y − 2 = 0, with L = f + λh. Find λ.
questions.x: Stationarity gives 2x + λ = 0 and 2y + λ = 0, so x = y = 1 and λ = −2.

questions.q: Same problem, now with constraint x + y = c and L = f + λ(x + y − c), λ = −2 at c = 2. Estimate, to first order, the change in f* when c goes from 2 to 2.1.
questions.x: df*/dc = −λ = 2, so Δf* ≈ 2 × 0.1 = 0.2 (the exact value c²/2 gives 0.205).

questions.q: Convention g ≤ 0, μ ≥ 0. A primal active-set QP method drops a constraint from the working set when
questions.a: Its multiplier estimate is negative
w: Its constraint value is strictly negative
It blocks the current step direction
The reduced Hessian becomes singular
questions.x: A negative multiplier shows f decreases by moving off that constraint into the interior, so the method releases it.

questions.q: The Fritz John conditions differ from KKT by
questions.a: A multiplier μ₀ ≥ 0 on ∇f that may equal 0
w: Dropping complementary slackness
Requiring LICQ at the candidate point
Using second derivatives of the constraints
questions.x: Fritz John holds at every local minimizer without a constraint qualification; under a CQ, μ₀ > 0 and scaling to μ₀ = 1 recovers KKT.

questions.q: Convention g ≤ 0. Two active constraints at x* have ∇g₁ = (1, 0) and ∇g₂ = (0, 1). KKT holds when −∇f lies
questions.a: In the cone spanned by (1, 0) and (0, 1)
w: In the cone spanned by (−1, 0) and (0, −1)
On the line through (1, 0) and (0, 1)
Orthogonal to both constraint gradients
questions.x: KKT requires −∇f = μ₁∇g₁ + μ₂∇g₂ with μ ≥ 0, so −∇f lies in the first quadrant cone of the active gradients.

questions.q: Complete the KKT system of min ½xᵀQx + cᵀx subject to Ax = b, with L = f + λᵀ(Ax − b)
questions.a: b
w: −b
Aᵀb
questions.x: Stationarity gives Qx + Aᵀλ = −c and feasibility gives Ax = b, forming one symmetric indefinite linear system.

questions.q: min x subject to g = x² ≤ 0, so the only feasible point is x* = 0. At x*
questions.a: LICQ fails and no KKT multiplier exists
w: KKT holds with μ = ½, since g is active at x*
KKT holds with μ = 0
LICQ holds since g is active
questions.x: ∇g = 2x vanishes at x* = 0, so ∇f = 1 has no representation −μ∇g; the minimizer satisfies Fritz John with μ₀ = 0.

questions.q: Convention g ≤ 0, so KKT requires μ ≥ 0. Match each multiplier and constraint state at a candidate point to its meaning
questions.x: Complementarity μg = 0 pairs positive multipliers with active constraints, and the multiplier sign shows whether the constraint holds f back.

questions.q: min x² subject to x = 1, using the quadratic penalty φ = x² + (μ/2)(x − 1)² with μ = 10. Give the minimizer of φ to 4 decimals.
questions.x: φ′ = 2x + μ(x − 1) = 0 gives x = μ/(2 + μ) = 0.8333, approaching 1 as μ grows.

questions.q: Method of multipliers for min x² subject to h = x − 1 = 0, L_A = x² + λh + (μ/2)h², with λ₀ = 0 and μ = 8. Minimize L_A, then update λ. Give λ₁.
questions.x: Minimizing gives x₁ = 0.8, and λ₁ = λ₀ + μh(x₁) = 8(−0.2) = −1.6, moving toward λ* = −2.

questions.q: The main advantage of the augmented Lagrangian over the quadratic penalty is that it
questions.a: Converges to x* with finite μ as λ approaches λ*
w: Keeps every iterate strictly feasible throughout the run
Removes the need for any inner minimization
Needs second derivatives only at the start
questions.x: The multiplier term shifts the penalty so the exact minimizer is reached at moderate μ, avoiding the ill-conditioning of μ → ∞.

questions.q: Complete the method of multipliers update for h(x) = 0 with L_A = f + λᵀh + (μ/2)‖h‖²
questions.a: μh(x_k)
w: h(x_k)/μ
μ∇h(x_k)
−μh(x_k)
questions.x: Stationarity of L_A gives ∇f + (λ_k + μh)ᵀ∇h = 0, so λ_k + μh(x_k) is the new multiplier estimate.

questions.q: In SQP with a line search, the merit function is used to
questions.a: Judge whether a step balances objective and feasibility
w: Build the quadratic model of the Lagrangian for the QP subproblem
Choose the active set for the QP subproblem
Replace the Hessian with a BFGS estimate
questions.x: A merit function such as f + ρ‖c‖₁ combines objective and constraint violation into one quantity the line search can decrease.

questions.q: A filter method accepts a trial point when
questions.a: No stored pair dominates its (f, violation)
w: Its ℓ1 merit value decreases by the Armijo condition
It lowers f, whatever its violation
Its constraint violation is exactly zero
questions.x: The filter treats objective and constraint violation as two goals and accepts points that improve one of them relative to every stored pair.

questions.q: The Maratos effect in SQP refers to
questions.a: A merit function rejecting good full steps near x*
w: The QP subproblem becoming infeasible far from the solution
Multipliers diverging when LICQ holds
The BFGS update losing positive definiteness
questions.x: Near x* the full SQP step can raise a nonsmooth merit function through second-order constraint curvature; a second-order correction step restores fast convergence.

questions.q: Put the augmented Lagrangian (method of multipliers) loop in order
steps: Minimize L_A(x; λ_k, μ_k) over x
Increase μ if ‖h‖ fell too little
questions.x: Each outer iteration minimizes the augmented Lagrangian, updates the multipliers from the constraint residual and raises μ only when feasibility progress stalls.

questions.q: Match each radial basis function to its form, with r = ‖x − c‖
questions.x: Gaussian and inverse multiquadric kernels give positive definite interpolation matrices; multiquadric and thin-plate splines are paired with a low-order polynomial tail.

questions.q: Gaussian RBF φ(r) = exp(−(εr)²) with ε = 1. Compute the kernel value between centres (0, 0) and (1, 1) to 4 decimals.
A kriging model predicts μ(x) = f_min exactly, with standard error σ = 2. Compute the expected improvement to 3 decimals.
questions.x: EI = (f_min − μ)Φ(z) + σφ(z) with z = 0 gives σ/√(2π) = 0.798.

questions.q: With n samples, leave-one-out cross-validation compared with 10-fold
questions.a: Needs n fits; nearly unbiased but higher variance
w: Needs 10 fits; biased toward larger error than any k-fold scheme
Needs n² fits; lowest variance of all
Needs one fit; identical to training error
questions.x: Leaving out one point uses n − 1 points per fit, giving a nearly unbiased error estimate with higher variance than k-fold.

questions.q: Complete the PRESS statistic, where ŷ₍₋ᵢ₎ is the model fit without sample i
questions.a: ŷ₍₋ᵢ₎(xᵢ)
w: ŷ(xᵢ)
ȳ
questions.x: PRESS sums the squared leave-one-out prediction errors at each held-out point.

questions.q: Solving least squares through the normal equations ΦᵀΦw = Φᵀy gives a condition number of
questions.a: κ(Φ)²
w: κ(Φ)
√κ(Φ)
2κ(Φ)
questions.x: Forming ΦᵀΦ squares the condition number, so QR or SVD on Φ itself is the numerically stable route.

questions.q: A full quadratic response surface in k = 20 variables needs at least how many samples?
questions.x: A full quadratic has (k + 1)(k + 2)/2 = 21·22/2 = 231 coefficients, an example of sample needs growing quickly with dimension.

questions.q: Kriging correlation parameters θ are usually chosen by
questions.a: Maximizing the concentrated likelihood
w: Least squares on training residuals
Fixing θ at the inverse sample spacing
Minimizing the predicted variance at x
questions.x: After the mean and process variance are profiled out, θ is found by maximizing the concentrated log likelihood, usually with a global optimizer.

questions.q: Forward difference error ≈ (h/2)|f″| + 2ε|f|/h. With ε = 10⁻¹⁶, |f| = 1, |f″| = 4, find the h that minimizes the error.
questions.x: Setting the derivative to zero gives h² = 4ε|f|/|f″| = 10⁻¹⁶, so h = 10⁻⁸, about √ε for a well-scaled f.

questions.q: Central difference for f(x) = x³ at x = 1 with h = 0.1. Give the result to 3 decimals.
questions.x: (1.1³ − 0.9³)/0.2 = 3.010, and the error h²f‴/6 = 0.01 matches the second-order truncation term.

questions.q: For a function with n inputs and m outputs, reverse-mode AD costs about
questions.a: m sweeps, each a small multiple of the cost of f
w: n sweeps, each a small multiple of the cost of f
One sweep, whatever the values of n and m
n·m sweeps, each the full cost of f
questions.x: Reverse mode yields one row of the Jacobian per sweep, so it suits many inputs and few outputs; forward mode yields one column per sweep.

questions.q: Jensen's inequality for convex f and random variable X states
questions.a: f(E[X]) ≤ E[f(X)]
w: f(E[X]) ≥ E[f(X)]
E[f(X)] ≤ f(E[X])²
E[f(X)] = f(E[X])
questions.x: For convex f the function of the mean lies at or below the mean of the function, with equality for affine f.

questions.q: Which composition is guaranteed convex?
questions.a: exp(g(x)) with g convex
w: √g(x) with g convex and positive
g(x)² with g convex
−ln g(x) with g convex and positive
questions.x: A convex nondecreasing outer function applied to a convex inner function is convex, and exp is convex and nondecreasing.

questions.q: Complete the direct (forward) method equation for du/dx with residuals R(x, u) = 0
w: ∂R/∂x
questions.x: Differentiating R(x, u(x)) = 0 gives one linear solve per design variable for du/dx.

questions.q: For a coupled aerostructural solver, the coupled adjoint system uses
questions.a: The transpose of the full coupled Jacobian ∂R/∂u
w: Separate adjoints with coupling terms set to zero
Finite differences of the converged coupling loop
The Jacobian of the aerodynamic residual only
questions.x: Stacking both disciplines' residuals gives one ∂R/∂u with off-diagonal coupling blocks, and its transpose defines the coupled adjoint.

questions.q: Put the adjoint computation of df/dx in order
steps: Solve R(x, u) = 0 for the state u
questions.x: One adjoint solve per function of interest gives its full gradient at a cost nearly independent of the number of design variables.

questions.q: Minimizing all objectives, design x₁ dominates x₂ when
questions.a: fᵢ(x₁) ≤ fᵢ(x₂) for all i, strictly for at least one
w: fᵢ(x₁) < fᵢ(x₂) for at least one objective i
Σᵢ fᵢ(x₁) < Σᵢ fᵢ(x₂) over all objectives
f₁(x₁) < f₁(x₂) with the other objectives free to vary
questions.x: Dominance means x₁ is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in one; the Pareto set is the nondominated designs.

questions.q: Minimize both objectives. Designs (f₁, f₂): (1,5), (2,3), (3,4), (4,1), (5,2). How many are Pareto optimal?
questions.x: (3,4) is dominated by (2,3) and (5,2) by (4,1), leaving (1,5), (2,3) and (4,1) on the front.

questions.q: Sweeping w in min w·f₁ + (1 − w)·f₂, with w in [0, 1], reaches
questions.a: Only points on convex portions of the Pareto front
w: Every Pareto point, given enough distinct weight values to sweep
Only the two anchor (single-objective) points
Dominated points close to the utopia point
questions.x: Each weight defines a supporting line to the front, so the weighted sum finds points on the convex hull of the front.

questions.q: The ε-constraint method
questions.a: Minimizes f₁ subject to f₂ ≤ ε, sweeping ε
w: Minimizes f₁ + ε·f₂, sweeping ε
Minimizes max(f₁, f₂) − ε at each step
Adds noise ε to each objective and resamples
questions.x: Turning all but one objective into constraints with swept bounds traces the full front, including nonconvex portions.

questions.q: The utopia point in objective space is
questions.a: The vector of each objective's own minimum
w: The Pareto point closest to the origin
The worst value of each objective on the front
The midpoint between the two anchor points
questions.x: Each component is the individual optimum of one objective; it is usually unattainable and serves as a reference for normalization and distance methods.

questions.q: Objectives are normalized before weighted-sum or distance methods so that
questions.a: Weights reflect preference, free of units and scale
w: The Pareto front becomes convex and easier to trace with weights
Every objective has the same minimizer
The number of objectives can be reduced
questions.x: Scaling each objective by its utopia and nadir values puts objectives on a common 0 to 1 range, so weights express trade-off preference.

questions.q: Match each genetic algorithm operator to its role
pairs: Picks parents with probability favouring fitness
Combines two parents' genes into offspring
Randomly perturbs genes to keep diversity
Copies the best designs into the next generation
questions.x: Selection and elitism drive exploitation, while crossover and mutation explore new regions of the design space.

questions.q: In PSO, v ← wv + c₁r₁(p_best − x) + c₂r₂(g_best − x). The c₁ term is the
questions.a: Cognitive pull toward the particle's own best
w: Social pull toward the best position found by the whole swarm
Inertia carrying the previous velocity
Random mutation of the particle position
questions.x: The c₁ term draws each particle toward its personal best, the c₂ term toward the swarm best, and w sets inertia.

questions.q: Complete the Metropolis criterion for an uphill move Δf > 0 at temperature T
questions.a: exp(−Δf/T)
w: exp(−T/Δf)
exp(Δf/T)
1 − Δf/T
questions.x: Downhill moves are always accepted and uphill moves are accepted with probability exp(−Δf/T), which shrinks as T falls.

questions.q: Simulated annealing at T = 1 proposes a move with Δf = 2. Compute the acceptance probability to 4 decimals.
As the temperature T → 0 in simulated annealing, the method
questions.a: Accepts only improving moves, like greedy descent
w: Accepts every proposed move, behaving like a pure random walk
Switches to gradient steps automatically
Restarts from the best design found so far
questions.x: exp(−Δf/T) → 0 for uphill moves as T → 0, so late stages refine locally; the cooling schedule, such as T_{k+1} = 0.9T_k, sets the pace from early exploration to late refinement.

questions.q: Put one Nelder-Mead iteration in order
steps: Order vertices by f and form the centroid of all but the worst
Reflect the worst vertex through the centroid
Expand if the reflected point beats the best vertex
Contract if the reflected point is still worse than the second worst
Shrink toward the best vertex if contraction fails
questions.x: Nelder-Mead reshapes the simplex with reflection, expansion, contraction and shrink using function values only.

questions.q: Nelder-Mead simplex with vertices (0,0), (2,0), (1,2), where (1,2) is worst. Reflect with coefficient 1. Give the y-coordinate of the reflected point.
questions.x: The centroid of (0,0) and (2,0) is (1,0), and x_r = c + (c − x_w) = (1, −2).

questions.q: DIRECT (dividing rectangles) chooses which boxes to divide by
questions.a: Selecting boxes potentially optimal for some Lipschitz constant
w: Sampling boxes uniformly at random across the domain each iteration
Dividing only the box that holds the current best
Estimating the gradient at each box centre point
questions.x: DIRECT divides every box on the lower right convex hull of (box size, centre value), balancing global and local search without a known Lipschitz constant.

questions.q: Gradient-free optimization is the better choice when f is
questions.a: Noisy or discrete, with few design variables
w: Smooth with an adjoint available and 1,000 variables
Convex with cheap exact gradients
High dimensional with analytic Hessians
questions.x: Gradient-free methods handle noise, discontinuities, discrete variables and multimodality, and their cost grows quickly with the number of variables.

questions.q: Complete the statement
questions.text: A Nelder-Mead simplex in n variables has ___ vertices
w: n
n²
questions.x: A simplex in n dimensions is the convex hull of n + 1 affinely independent points.

questions.q: A Gauss-Seidel multidisciplinary analysis differs from Jacobi in that
questions.a: Each discipline uses the latest coupling values at once
w: All disciplines run in parallel on the previous iteration's values
It solves the coupled residuals by Newton's method
It replaces each discipline with a surrogate model
questions.x: Gauss-Seidel passes updated coupling variables to the next discipline within the same sweep, which usually converges in fewer iterations than Jacobi.

questions.q: Newton's method for a multidisciplinary analysis
questions.a: Uses coupled partial derivatives and converges quadratically
w: Uses only discipline outputs and converges linearly like fixed point
Needs one discipline evaluation per outer sweep
Runs each discipline once with no iteration at all
questions.x: Newton solves the coupled residuals with the full Jacobian, including coupling blocks, and converges quadratically near the solution, also for strong coupling.

questions.q: Match each MDO architecture or tool to its description
pairs: Full MDA at every optimizer iteration
Coupling targets as design variables with consistency constraints
Discipline optimizers match targets set by a system optimizer
Sequential fixed-point solve of the couplings
questions.x: MDF keeps disciplines consistent at each iterate, IDF lets the optimizer enforce consistency, and CO distributes optimization to the disciplines.

questions.q: In IDF, disciplinary consistency is enforced by
questions.a: Constraints equating coupling targets and outputs
w: A full MDA run before each objective and constraint evaluation
A penalty on the variance across disciplines
Fixing coupling variables at initial values
questions.x: IDF adds coupling targets as design variables with equality constraints so disciplines run independently and in parallel at each iterate.

questions.q: Compared with IDF, MDF
questions.a: Has fewer variables and is consistent at every iterate
w: Has more variables and needs no multidisciplinary analysis at all
Runs all disciplines fully in parallel
Reaches consistency only at convergence
questions.x: MDF solves the coupled analysis for every design, so each iterate is multidisciplinary feasible and early termination still gives a consistent design.

questions.q: In an N² diagram with disciplines on the diagonal (outputs along rows, inputs along columns), entries below the diagonal show
questions.a: Feedback from later disciplines to earlier ones
w: Feedforward from earlier disciplines to later ones
Design variables shared by every discipline
Constraints applied at the system level
questions.x: Below-diagonal entries are feedback loops that require iteration; reordering disciplines to minimize them speeds the MDA.

questions.q: A full factorial design with 4 factors at 3 levels each. How many runs?
questions.x: A full factorial needs levels^factors = 3⁴ = 81 runs.

questions.q: A central composite design for k = 4 factors with 3 center points. How many runs?
Complete the central composite design run count for k factors and n_c center points
questions.a: 2k
w: k²
2ᵏ⁻¹
k
questions.x: A CCD combines 2ᵏ factorial corners, 2k axial (star) points and n_c center points, enough to fit a full quadratic.

questions.q: In a resolution III fractional factorial design
questions.a: Main effects are aliased with two-factor interactions
w: Main effects are aliased with other main effects
Two-factor interactions are entirely free of aliasing
Main effects alias only with three-factor interactions
questions.x: Resolution III keeps main effects clear of each other and aliases them with two-factor interactions; resolution IV clears them of two-factor interactions.

questions.q: A 2² design gives y(A−,B−) = 10, y(A+,B−) = 14, y(A−,B+) = 12, y(A+,B+) = 20. Compute the main effect of A.
questions.x: Main effect of A = mean at A+ minus mean at A− = (14 + 20)/2 − (10 + 12)/2 = 17 − 11 = 6.

questions.q: A nonzero AB interaction in a two-level factorial means
questions.a: The effect of A depends on the level of B
w: A and B have equal main effects
A and B are aliased with each other in the design
The response is linear in A and B
questions.x: The interaction is half the difference between the effect of A at B+ and at B−, so it measures how one factor changes the other's effect.

questions.q: Reliability-based design optimization replaces the constraint g(x) ≤ 0 with
questions.a: P[g(x, U) > 0] ≤ P_f,allow
w: g(x, E[U]) ≤ 0 at the mean inputs
g(x, U) ≤ 0 for one sampled U
E[g(x, U)] ≤ 0 over the inputs
questions.x: RBDO bounds the probability of failure under uncertain inputs U, often through the reliability index β from FORM.

questions.q: In ANOVA, a factor is judged significant when
questions.a: Its F = MS_factor/MS_error exceeds F_crit
w: Its sum of squares exceeds the total sum of squares
Its mean square falls below the error mean square
Its main effect has a positive sign
questions.x: The F ratio compares variance explained by the factor with error variance, and a value above the critical F at the chosen significance level marks significance.

questions.q: Complete the Monte Carlo standard error of a sample mean with N samples
questions.a: √N
w: N
N²
ln N
questions.x: Monte Carlo error falls as 1/√N independent of dimension, so halving the error takes four times the samples.

questions.q: Match each design of experiments to its structure
pairs: Factorial corners plus axial and center points
Edge midpoints plus center points, no corners
One sample in each stratum of each variable
questions.x: Factorial-based designs suit response surfaces in few factors, Box-Behnken avoids extreme corners, and Latin hypercubes spread samples for computer experiments.

boards.prompt: H = [[3,1],[1,3]] and b = 0. Find the eigenvectors by hand, sketch the contours and tell me which axis is longer. Now flip the off-diagonal entries to −1: what changes?
points: Eigenvectors are (1,1)/√2 with λ = 4 and (1,−1)/√2 with λ = 2, at 45° because the diagonal entries are equal
Contours are ellipses with semi-axis proportional to 1/√λ, so the long axis lies along (1,−1)
With off-diagonals −1 the eigenvalues stay 2 and 4 and the eigenvectors swap, so the long axis moves to (1,1)
Along an eigendirection f − f* = ½λα², which gives the curvature in that direction

boards.prompt: Classify every contour family a two-variable quadratic can produce. Now take f = x² + y: what do the contours look like and is there a minimum?
points: Positive definite H gives ellipses around a unique minimizer
Indefinite H gives hyperbolas around a saddle point
Singular PSD H with b in the range of H gives parallel lines and a whole line of minimizers
f = x² + y has a zero eigenvalue along y with b = (0,1) in the null space, so the contours are parabolas y = c − x²

boards.prompt: Draw φ(α) for a descent direction and shade the step lengths accepted by the weak Wolfe conditions. Now switch to strong Wolfe: what changes in your picture?
points: Sufficient decrease keeps steps with φ(α) on or below the line φ(0) + c₁αφ′(0)
The weak curvature condition keeps steps with φ′(α) ≥ c₂φ′(0), removing tiny steps
Strong Wolfe adds φ′(α) ≤ c₂|φ′(0)|, removing steps where φ is climbing steeply
Strong Wolfe intervals cluster around the local minimizers of φ
Typical constants are c₁ = 10⁻⁴ and c₂ = 0.9 for quasi-Newton, c₂ = 0.1 for nonlinear CG

boards.prompt: Your steepest descent code takes thousands of iterations on a smooth problem. What is going on, and what are your options?
points: The rate is linear with worst-case factor ((κ−1)/(κ+1))², so a large condition number κ makes progress slow
The iterates zigzag because successive exact-line-search directions are orthogonal
Rescaling the variables or preconditioning reduces κ
Switching to conjugate gradients, BFGS or Newton gives faster rates using curvature information

boards.prompt: Derive the BFGS update starting from the secant condition. Now your line search hands you a step with yᵀs < 0: what do you do?
points: The secant condition is B₊s = y, matching the gradient change along the step
BFGS chooses the symmetric inverse H₊ closest to H in a weighted Frobenius norm subject to H₊y = s, a rank-two update
B₊ stays positive definite exactly when yᵀs > 0
The Wolfe curvature condition guarantees yᵀs > 0, so a proper line search prevents the problem
Otherwise skip the update or use Powell damping, which blends y with Bs to restore positive curvature

boards.prompt: Run linear CG by hand on a 2x2 SPD quadratic. Now the Hessian has condition number 10⁴: how many iterations do you expect and what do you do?
points: CG terminates in at most 2 iterations for a 2x2 SPD system in exact arithmetic
Search directions are A-conjugate and residuals are mutually orthogonal
For large systems the error shrinks roughly by (√κ − 1)/(√κ + 1) per iteration, about 0.98 for κ = 10⁴
Preconditioning clusters the eigenvalues of the preconditioned matrix and cuts the iteration count

boards.prompt: Write the trust region subproblem and its exact optimality conditions. Now B is indefinite and g = 0: what does the solution look like?
points: The subproblem is min m(p) = f + gᵀp + ½pᵀBp subject to ‖p‖ ≤ Δ
The solution satisfies (B + λI)p = −g, λ ≥ 0, λ(Δ − ‖p‖) = 0 and B + λI positive semidefinite
With g = 0 and indefinite B, p = ±Δv along the eigenvector of the most negative eigenvalue, with λ = −λ_min
This step moves the iterate off a saddle point, which a pure Newton step would stay on

boards.prompt: Compare the dogleg method and Steihaug-CG. Which do you use for 10⁵ variables where you only have Hessian-vector products?
points: Dogleg combines the Cauchy point and the full step p_B = −B⁻¹g, needing B positive definite and a factorization
Steihaug-CG needs only Hessian-vector products and handles indefinite B by stopping at the boundary on negative curvature
Its first CG iterate is the Cauchy point, so it achieves at least Cauchy decrease
For 10⁵ variables with Hessian-vector products only, Steihaug-CG is the method of choice

boards.prompt: Minimize x² + y² subject to x + y = 2 by hand using a Lagrange multiplier. Now change the right-hand side to 2.1: predict the new optimum value without re-solving.
points: Stationarity of L = f + λ(x + y − 2) gives 2x + λ = 0, 2y + λ = 0, so x = y = 1, λ = −2, f* = 2
At the optimum ∇f is parallel to ∇h, the normal of the constraint line
The sensitivity is df*/dc = −λ = 2 with this sign convention
The first-order prediction is f* ≈ 2 + 2(0.1) = 2.2, against the exact 2.205

boards.prompt: Explain how an active-set method solves a convex inequality-constrained QP. Now the problem has thousands of inequalities: what would you change?
points: A working set of constraints is treated as equalities and the equality QP is solved through its KKT system
If the step hits a blocking constraint, the method takes the feasible fraction and adds that constraint
If the step is zero and a multiplier is negative, that constraint leaves the working set
Each change of working set alters one constraint, so iterations can grow with the number of constraints
Interior point methods handle many inequalities with an iteration count that grows slowly with problem size

boards.prompt: Take min x² subject to x = 1. Run one iteration of the method of multipliers by hand with μ = 8 and λ₀ = 0. Now tell me why this beats the pure quadratic penalty.
points: Minimizing x² + λ₀(x − 1) + 4(x − 1)² gives x₁ = 0.8
The update λ₁ = λ₀ + μh(x₁) = −1.6 moves toward λ* = −2
Pure penalty reaches x* only as μ → ∞, and the Hessian condition number grows like μ
The augmented Lagrangian reaches x* with finite μ, so the subproblems stay well conditioned

boards.prompt: Your SQP steps look great, but the line search keeps cutting them near the solution. What is happening and how do you fix it?
points: This is the Maratos effect: the full step raises the ℓ1 merit function through constraint curvature
Superlinear convergence needs the unit step to be accepted near x*
A second-order correction step projects back toward the constraints and restores acceptance
A watchdog (nonmonotone) strategy or a filter method also accepts the full steps

boards.prompt: Write expected improvement for a kriging model and explain how it trades exploration against exploitation. Now what is EI at a point you have already sampled?
points: EI = (f_min − μ)Φ(z) + σφ(z) with z = (f_min − μ)/σ
The first term rewards a low predicted mean (exploitation)
The second term rewards high predicted uncertainty (exploration)
Noise-free kriging interpolates, so σ = 0 and EI = 0 at a sampled point
Maximizing EI selects each new infill sample, as in efficient global optimization (EGO)

boards.prompt: You fit a Gaussian RBF interpolant and the weight solve blows up. Why? Then tell me how you choose the shape parameter.
points: The Gaussian kernel matrix becomes ill-conditioned as ε → 0 or as centres crowd together
A small ridge term λI or a larger ε restores conditioning at some cost in interpolation
Thin-plate splines with a polynomial tail avoid a shape parameter
The shape parameter is chosen by minimizing leave-one-out error, which has a cheap closed form for RBFs (Rippa's formula)

boards.prompt: Derive the optimal step size for a forward difference in double precision. Now compare central differences and the complex step.
points: Forward difference error is truncation (h/2)|f″| plus subtractive cancellation of about 2ε|f|/h
Balancing the two gives h ≈ 2√(ε|f|/|f″|), about 10⁻⁸ for a well-scaled f, with about half the digits accurate
Central differences have O(h²) truncation error and optimal h near ε^(1/3), about 10⁻⁵
Complex step f′ ≈ Im f(x + ih)/h has no subtraction, so h = 10⁻²⁰⁰ gives derivatives to machine precision
Each finite difference or complex step gradient costs about n function evaluations

boards.prompt: Explain forward and reverse mode automatic differentiation. Now you have a coupled aerostructural solver with 300 design variables and 3 outputs: how do you get the gradients?
points: Forward mode propagates derivatives with the computation and gives one Jacobian column per sweep
Reverse mode propagates adjoints backward and gives one Jacobian row per sweep, storing the forward trace
With 300 inputs and 3 outputs, reverse mode or the adjoint method needs about 3 solves
The coupled adjoint uses the transpose of the full coupled Jacobian, including discipline coupling blocks
AD can supply the partial derivatives ∂R/∂u and ∂R/∂x that the adjoint system needs

boards.prompt: Draw objective space for two competing objectives and mark the Pareto front, the utopia point and a dominated design. Now the front is nonconvex: which scalarization do you use?
points: The Pareto front is the set of nondominated designs, the lower left boundary when minimizing both
The utopia point collects each objective's individual minimum and lies outside the feasible region for conflicting objectives
A dominated design has another design at least as good in every objective and better in one
A weighted sum reaches only convex portions of the front
The ε-constraint method or normal boundary intersection traces nonconvex portions

boards.prompt: Walk me through one generation of a genetic algorithm. How do you handle constraints, and how many function evaluations should I expect?
points: Evaluate the population, select parents by fitness (tournament or roulette), apply crossover and mutation, and keep elites
Constraints enter through penalties or feasibility rules that rank feasible designs above infeasible ones
Total evaluations equal population size times generations, often thousands
Each generation evaluates in parallel, which suits expensive analyses on a cluster
NSGA-II extends the GA to multiple objectives with nondominated sorting and crowding distance

boards.prompt: Explain simulated annealing and its acceptance rule. Now what does the cooling schedule control?
points: A random neighbour is proposed; downhill moves are always accepted
Uphill moves are accepted with Metropolis probability exp(−Δf/T)
High T allows escape from local minima and broad exploration
The cooling schedule, such as geometric T_{k+1} = αT_k with α near 0.9 to 0.99, sets the exploration to refinement trade-off
Slow logarithmic cooling gives convergence to the global optimum in probability

boards.prompt: When would you choose a gradient-free method over a gradient-based one for an aircraft design problem? Now the problem grows to 500 variables.
points: Gradient-free suits noisy, discontinuous or discrete problems, multimodal landscapes and few variables
Gradient-free cost grows rapidly with the number of variables
Gradient-based methods with adjoint derivatives scale to hundreds of variables at nearly fixed gradient cost
For 500 variables, use gradient-based optimization with adjoints, with multistart for multimodality
A hybrid uses a global gradient-free search to find a basin, then gradient-based refinement

boards.prompt: Draw an N² diagram for aerodynamics, structures and performance in a wing design. Now set up MDF and IDF for it and tell me which you would pick.
points: Aerodynamics passes loads to structures and structures passes deflections back, forming a feedback loop
Performance receives drag and weight as feedforward inputs
MDF converges the aerostructural MDA for each design, so every iterate is consistent
IDF adds load and displacement targets as variables with consistency constraints, allowing parallel discipline runs
MDF suits a robust, available MDA solver; IDF suits strong coupling with costly or separately owned disciplines

boards.prompt: Solve the coupled aerostructural analysis. Compare Gauss-Seidel and Newton for the MDA. Now the coupling is strong: what happens?
points: Gauss-Seidel iterates disciplines in sequence using the latest coupling values and converges linearly
Newton solves the coupled residual system with the full Jacobian and converges quadratically
Strong coupling slows or stalls the fixed-point iteration; Aitken relaxation helps
Newton handles strong coupling well and its Jacobian is reused in the coupled adjoint

boards.prompt: You have 4 factors and a budget of 30 runs to fit a quadratic response surface. Which design do you pick? Now one factor is a noise variable: how do you make the design robust?
points: A full quadratic in 4 factors has 15 coefficients
A three-level full factorial needs 3⁴ = 81 runs, beyond the budget
A central composite design needs 16 + 8 + n_c runs, about 27, and fits a quadratic
Box-Behnken with 4 factors needs 27 runs including 3 center points
For robustness, cross control factors with the noise factor (Taguchi inner and outer arrays) and maximize S/N, or model mean and variance directly

boards.prompt: Propagate input uncertainty through your design and set up an RBDO problem. How many Monte Carlo samples do you need for a failure probability near 10⁻³?
points: Monte Carlo error scales as 1/√N regardless of dimension
The coefficient of variation of the P_f estimate is √((1 − P_f)/(N·P_f)), so 10% error at 10⁻³ needs about 10⁵ samples
FORM finds the most probable point and gives P_f ≈ Φ(−β) from the reliability index β
RBDO minimizes cost subject to P[gᵢ > 0] ≤ P_f,allow for each failure mode
Decoupled methods such as SORA replace the nested double loop with a sequence of deterministic problems
